title: Add security group patterns for private ingress/egress (EKS + installer-friendly outputs)
author: Bruno Silva
description: This PR introduces an opinionated set of Security Group (SG) modules/patterns for Redwood Private AWS deployments (alpha). The intent is to reduce pilot variability and common discovery churn by shipping Redwood-validated defaults for: (1) EKS worker/node SG behavior (private nodes), (2) load balancer SGs for internal ingress (ALB/NLB) and controlled cross-subnet traffic, and (3) egress policy that works in a mostly-private VPC with VPC endpoints (ECR/S3/STS/CloudWatch Logs, etc.). Key goals: keep the default posture secure (no accidental broad public egress), but avoid breaking real-world installs where customers still need proxy/NAT-based egress or have non-standard endpoint/DNS setups. The modules are designed to be composable and to expose controlled extension points (additional egress CIDRs, additional destination SGs, and an explicit opt-in for “wide egress”). Summary of changes: Added new module `modules/security-groups` with submodules `eks_nodes`, `internal_lb`, and `egress`. Added a shared `rules` helper to centralize common TCP/UDP rules and keep diffs readable. Default node SG: ingress from cluster SG (EKS-managed), ingress from internal LB SG on app ports (configurable list, default 443), and egress constrained to VPC endpoints (via prefix lists and endpoint ENI SGs) + DNS + NTP (optional). Default internal LB SG: ingress from allowlisted CIDRs / SGs (supports customer VPN/DX CIDRs) and egress only to node SG on configured target ports. Default egress SG pattern: supports two modes: (a) “endpoint-only” (default) where 443 egress is restricted to endpoint prefix lists and/or endpoint SG IDs, and (b) “wide” where 0.0.0.0/0 egress on 443 is allowed for customers who require NAT/proxy access during bring-up (explicit input `enable_wide_egress = true`, default false). Outputs: `node_security_group_id`, `internal_lb_security_group_id`, `egress_security_group_id`, plus lists for per-rule debugging to make installer preflight messages actionable. Example usage added to `examples/alpha/private-eks-vpc/` and referenced in README. Notes: This PR does not attempt to model every enterprise firewall topology; instead, it standardizes the baseline and provides extension points. In particular, customers with explicit proxy egress can attach the egress SG to proxy ENIs or override via `additional_egress_*` inputs. Checklist: [x] Terraform fmt/validate; [x] tflint; [x] checkov (with documented suppressions where appropriate); [x] example plan applies in sandbox; [x] docs updated for supported extension points; [x] aligns with installer expectations for private image pulls (ECR/S3/STSv2).
commits: feat(security-groups): add base SG rule helpers and naming conventions
feat(modules/security-groups): add eks_nodes SG pattern with controlled ingress + endpoint-first egress
feat(modules/security-groups): add internal_lb SG pattern for private ALB/NLB to node targets
feat(modules/security-groups): add egress SG pattern with endpoint-only default + explicit wide-egress opt-in
docs(examples): wire SG module into alpha private EKS example and update README inputs/outputs
chore(ci): tighten checkov config and add tests for SG rule generation
ci_checks: checkov: pass (2 suppressions added with justification)
conversation: Victor Alvarez (review): The module shape looks good, but we need to be careful about the semantic meaning of “egress SG” in AWS. If customers attach multiple SGs to nodes, AWS unions the rules—so the secure default can be defeated by attaching a permissive SG elsewhere. Can we make the default still safe while not pretending it’s enforced? Also, can we prefer endpoint ENI SG IDs over prefix lists where possible? Bruno Silva (author): Agree. I added language to the module README: ‘This module provides a secure baseline but cannot prevent additional SG attachments.’ For endpoints, the module now supports both `endpoint_prefix_list_ids` and `endpoint_security_group_ids` and encourages endpoint SGs when customers own them. Marcus Lin (security review): Strong request: default must not allow 0.0.0.0/0 egress. We’ve seen pilots where “temporary” wide egress becomes permanent. If we need a break-glass option, it must be explicit and loud. Also, do not allow all VPC CIDR by default unless justified. Bruno Silva (author): Updated defaults: `enable_wide_egress` is false and guarded; when true we tag the SG with `redwood.io/wide-egress=true` and print a warning in README + example. Removed default allow-to-vpc-cidr egress; it’s now `additional_egress_cidrs` (empty by default). Nina Petrova (private deployments): For EKS private control plane, ensure nodes can reach the cluster endpoint and CoreDNS resolution works consistently. Some customers use VPC resolver endpoints; others rely on the default AmazonProvidedDNS. We should avoid overfitting. Bruno Silva (author): Node SG egress includes UDP/TCP 53 to the VPC resolver address range via `dns_egress_cidrs` input (defaults to the VPC CIDR, with clear guidance to set it to resolver endpoint IPs when used). Control plane connectivity remains governed by EKS-managed cluster SG rules; our module expects `cluster_security_group_id` as input and adds required ingress from that SG. Irene Choi (infra): The initial version had separate SGs per endpoint. That’s too many moving pieces for alpha. Please keep it to three SGs max and make the extension points straightforward. Bruno Silva (author): Simplified: three SGs as described (nodes/internal-lb/egress). Endpoints are referenced as destinations rather than modeled as their own SGs (optional input if customer provides endpoint SG IDs). Sean Gallagher (SRE): Concern about operability: in practice, debugging broken installs is easier when there’s a quick ‘make it work’ path. Can we support a temporary egress mode without rewriting code? Bruno Silva (author): Added `enable_wide_egress` + `wide_egress_ports` (default [443]) and documented a recommended rollback plan: start endpoint-only, only enable wide egress for initial bring-up if required, then revert once endpoints/proxy are validated. Hanae Suzuki (security templates): checkov is flagging ingress rules that depend on user-provided CIDRs. That’s fine, but we need strong validation and examples. Bruno Silva (author): Added variable validation: CIDRs must be valid and non-empty; added example showing allowlisting a VPN CIDR and a customer bastion SG; added checkov suppressions only for the module that intentionally supports customer-provided allowlists, with justification text. Final outcome: approvals from Victor + Marcus after tightening defaults and documenting the break-glass path; merged after CI green.
release_notes: Alpha: Added opinionated security group modules for Redwood Private AWS VPC deployments (EKS nodes, internal load balancers, and endpoint-first egress). Default posture avoids broad public egress; provides explicit opt-in for temporary wide egress when required during bring-up.
